table.caption: Standard molar entropy S° of nine substances at 298 K

entropy-change-s2.title: Entropy of substance Q as it is heated
entropy-change-s2.text: A chemist measures the molar entropy of a pure substance Q from 0 K to 400 K at constant pressure. Q melts at 200 K and boils at 320 K.

items.q: Calculate ΔS° for the reaction N₂(g) + 3 H₂(g) → 2 NH₃(g).

mistakes.why: Value: you left out the coefficients. Multiply each S° by its coefficient: 2 for NH₃ and 3 for H₂.
Value: you used the coefficient for NH₃ but not the 3 for H₂.
Units: the table is in J/(mol·K), so the answer is in J/(mol·K) unless you convert on purpose.

why.correct: ΔS° = Σ nS°(products) − Σ nS°(reactants) = 2(192.8) − [191.6 + 3(130.7)] = 385.6 − 583.7 = −198.1 J/(mol·K). Each value is known to 0.1, so the answer keeps one decimal place. The sign fits the prediction: 4 mol of gas become 2 mol.

items.q: Calculate ΔS° for the combustion of methane at 298 K: CH₄(g) + 2 O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2 H₂O(l).

mistakes.why: Value: you used S° for H₂O(g). The equation makes liquid water, so use 69.9 J/(mol·K).
Value: you left out the coefficients of 2 on H₂O and O₂.

why.correct: ΔS° = [213.8 + 2(69.9)] − [186.3 + 2(205.2)] = 353.6 − 596.7 = −243.1 J/(mol·K). Three moles of gas become one mole of gas plus a liquid, so the large negative value makes sense.

items.q: If the water in the combustion of methane were formed as a gas instead of a liquid, ΔS° would be −5.3 J/(mol·K) instead of −243.1 J/(mol·K). Which statement explains the difference?
options: Making a gas releases less heat, and less heat released means more entropy for the products.
Gaseous water molecules spread through the whole container, so H₂O(g) has far more microstates.
The version that makes water vapor has fewer moles of products, so its ΔS° is closer to zero.
H₂O(g) has a larger molar mass than H₂O(l), so each mole of the gas carries more entropy.

why.correct: Only the phase of the water changes. Gas molecules are far more dispersed, so S°(H₂O(g)) is much larger, and ΔS° is less negative.
options: This mixes up enthalpy and entropy. The difference comes from the S° values of the two phases of water.
Right: S°(H₂O(g)) is 188.8 against 69.9 for the liquid, because the gas molecules are dispersed.
The moles of product are the same (1 CO₂ + 2 H₂O) either way; only the phase of the water differs.
The molar mass of water is 18.02 g/mol in every phase. The phase changes the number of arrangements, not the mass.

items.q: Calculate ΔS° for the vaporization of one mole of water at 298 K, H₂O(l) → H₂O(g).

why.correct: ΔS° = S°(H₂O(g)) − S°(H₂O(l)) = 188.8 − 69.9 = 118.9 J/(mol·K). Positive, as expected when a liquid becomes a gas.

items.q: Using your answer for N₂(g) + 3 H₂(g) → 2 NH₃(g), calculate ΔS° for 4 NH₃(g) → 2 N₂(g) + 6 H₂(g).

mistakes.why: Value: you reversed the reaction but did not double it. ΔS° is extensive: twice the amount of reaction, twice the entropy change.
Value: you doubled ΔS° but kept its sign. Reversing a reaction flips the sign of ΔS°.

why.correct: This is the original reaction reversed (sign flips) and doubled (value doubles): ΔS° = −2 × (−198.1) = 396.2 J/(mol·K).

items.q: Why is the entropy of Q zero at 0 K?
options: At 0 K the substance has no mass left, so there is nothing to have entropy.
Entropy is set to zero for any pure substance in its standard state, as ΔH°f is for elements.
At 0 K the particles move fastest, so they spend no time at any single place in the crystal.
A perfect crystal at 0 K has one arrangement of its particles and energy: a single microstate.

why.correct: A perfect crystal at 0 K has only one way to arrange its particles and energy, so S = 0. Every substance above 0 K has positive entropy.
options: Mass does not disappear on cooling. The particles are still there, just in a single arrangement.
That is true of ΔH°f for elements, not of entropy. S° of every substance at 298 K is positive.
At 0 K the particles have the least possible motion, not the most.
Right: one microstate means zero entropy. This is the third law of thermodynamics.

items.q: Use the graph to find the entropy change when one mole of Q boils at 320 K.

mistakes.why: Value: that is the jump at the melting point (200 K). Boiling is the jump at 320 K.
Value: that is the entropy of the gas at 320 K. The change is the height of the jump, final minus initial.

why.correct: At 320 K the entropy jumps from 91 to 180 J/(mol·K): ΔS = 180 − 91 = 89 J/(mol·K).

items.q: The jump in entropy at the boiling point is much larger than the jump at the melting point. Which is the best explanation?
options: On boiling, particles go from touching to filling the whole container: a far larger gain in arrangements than melting gives.
Boiling happens at the higher temperature, and a higher temperature gives a larger jump for any phase change of Q.
Boiling breaks the covalent bonds inside the particles of Q, while melting leaves those bonds intact.
The gas is more disordered than the liquid, while the solid and the liquid are about equally disordered.

why.correct: In a liquid the particles still touch; in a gas they spread through the whole container. That change gives far more new microstates than melting does.
options: Right: the volume available to each particle grows enormously on boiling, so the gain in microstates is much larger.
The temperature is not why. The size of the jump comes from how much more freely the particles move in the new phase.
Neither melting nor boiling breaks covalent bonds; both overcome attractions between particles.
"Disordered" gives no particle-level cause, and the solid and liquid differ too, as the jump at 200 K shows.

items.q: Between 250 K and 300 K, Q stays a liquid but its entropy still rises. Why?
options: Some of the liquid freezes as it is heated, adding solid particles to the sample of Q.
The liquid particles lose energy as they are heated, so they end up more spread out.
Their energy spreads over a wider range of speeds, giving more ways to share it.
The number of moles of Q in the sample increases as the liquid warms up.

why.correct: Within a phase, adding energy widens the spread of particle speeds. More ways to distribute the energy means higher entropy.
options: Heating does not freeze a liquid; the sample stays liquid in this range.
Heating adds energy to the particles; it does not remove it.
Right: within one phase, entropy rises with temperature because energy disperses over more microstates.
Heating does not create matter; the amount of Q is fixed.

items.q: Which statement about standard molar entropies at 298 K is correct?
options: Elements in their standard states have S° = 0, just as they have ΔH°f = 0.
Solids have negative S° values, liquids have zero, and gases have positive S° values.
Every pure substance, elements in their standard states included, has S° > 0.
S° is given in kJ/mol, the same energy unit as ΔH°f values are.

why.correct: S° is an absolute value measured up from zero at 0 K, so it is positive for every pure substance at 298 K, elements included.
options: This confuses S° with ΔH°f. ΔH°f of an element is zero by definition; S° is measured from 0 K and is positive.
S° values are measured from a perfect crystal at 0 K, so they are all positive; solids are simply the smallest.
Right: any substance above 0 K has some motion and so more than one microstate.
S° is in J/(mol·K): joules, not kilojoules, and per kelvin.

items.q: Without a table, which substance has the largest standard molar entropy at 298 K?
options: C₂H₆(g)
C(s, diamond)
H₂O(l)
CH₄(g)

why.correct: Gases beat liquids and solids. Between two gases, the molecule with more atoms has more ways to rotate and vibrate.
options: Right: a gas, and a molecule with eight atoms, so it has the most ways to store energy.
A rigid network solid has very few microstates: its S° is among the smallest of all substances.
A liquid has more entropy than a solid but much less than a gas.
A gas, but with fewer atoms per molecule than C₂H₆, so fewer ways to store energy.

items.q: For 2 NO(g) + O₂(g) → 2 NO₂(g), ΔS° = −146.6 J/(mol·K). S° is 210.8 J/(mol·K) for NO(g) and 205.2 J/(mol·K) for O₂(g). Calculate S° of NO₂(g).

mistakes.why: Value: that is the total for 2 mol of NO₂. Divide by the coefficient 2 to get S° for one mole.
Value: check the sign of ΔS°. Rearranging 2S°(NO₂) − 626.8 = −146.6 gives 2S°(NO₂) = 480.2.

items.q: Calculate ΔS° for CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g). S° values in J/(mol·K): CaCO₃(s) 91.7, CaO(s) 38.1, CO₂(g) 213.8.

mistakes.why: Sign: you subtracted products from reactants. ΔS° = Σ S°(products) − Σ S°(reactants).

why.correct: ΔS° = (38.1 + 213.8) − 91.7 = 160.2 J/(mol·K). A gas forms from a solid, so ΔS° is large and positive.

items.q: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes: 2 H₂O₂(l) → 2 H₂O(l) + O₂(g). S° values in J/(mol·K): H₂O₂(l) 109.6, H₂O(l) 69.9, O₂(g) 205.2. Calculate ΔS°.

mistakes.why: Value: you left out the coefficients of 2 on H₂O₂ and H₂O.

items.q: A student calculates ΔS° = +38.4 J/(mol·K) for 2 SO₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2 SO₃(g). Without redoing the arithmetic, why should the student doubt this result?
options: SO₃ is a heavier molecule than SO₂, so ΔS° should be zero.
Combination reactions release heat, so ΔS° should be larger than +38.4.
ΔS° values are given in kJ, so a value as large as 38.4 is impossible.
Three moles of gas become two, so ΔS° should be negative.

why.correct: Always check the sign of a calculated ΔS° against the change in moles of gas. Here 3 mol of gas → 2 mol of gas, so ΔS° < 0 (the true value is about −188 J/(mol·K)).
options: Molar mass does not set ΔS° to zero; the change in moles of gas decides the sign here.
Heat released is ΔH, not ΔS. The drop in moles of gas makes ΔS° negative.
Entropy changes are given in J/(mol·K), and values of tens to hundreds are typical.
Right: fewer gas particles means fewer microstates, so a positive answer signals an error (here, missing coefficients or a sign slip).

items.q: For which reaction is it hardest to predict the sign of ΔS° without a table of S° values?
options: 2 H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2 H₂O(g)
H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2 HCl(g)
NH₄Cl(s) → NH₃(g) + HCl(g)
C₃H₈(g) + 5 O₂(g) → 3 CO₂(g) + 4 H₂O(g)

why.correct: When the moles of gas and the phases do not change, ΔS° is small and the S° values are needed to decide its sign.
options: Three moles of gas become two, so ΔS° is clearly negative.
Right: 2 mol of gas on each side and no phase change, so the change is small and its sign is not obvious.
A solid makes two moles of gas, so ΔS° is clearly positive.
Six moles of gas become seven, so ΔS° is positive.

items.q: A reaction has ΔS° = −120 J/(mol·K). A student needs this value in the same energy unit as ΔH° = −92 kJ/mol. What is ΔS° in that unit?
options: −1.20 kJ/(mol·K)
−393 kJ/(mol·K)

why.correct: ΔS° tables use joules; ΔH° tables use kilojoules. 120 J = 0.120 kJ, so ΔS° = −0.120 kJ/(mol·K). You will need this conversion in topic 9.3.
options: Right: divide joules by 1000 to get kilojoules.
Converting J to kJ means dividing by 1000, not multiplying.
That divides by 100. One kilojoule is 1000 joules.
That subtracts 273 from the value, as if converting a temperature. Only the energy unit changes.
